en: Theragāthā 9.1 Navaka-nipāta Paṭhama-vagga (The First Chapter)
The Bhūta Thera’s Verse:
“When the wise man understands that aging and death are suffering—
yet where ordinary people, lacking true knowledge, remain bound.”
Having fully understood suffering, one meditates with mindfulness;
therefore, one finds no greater delight than that.
When one has abandoned the attachment that brings about suffering,
Having abandoned craving, which brings about the mass of conceptual proliferation and carries with it suffering,
the mindful one meditates; he finds no greater delight than that.
When, having seen with wisdom the auspicious,
supreme path leading to the two and four fruits,
which purifies all defilements, one meditates mindful and alert,
One finds no greater delight than this:
when one reaches the sorrowless, stainless,
unconditioned state— peaceful and the purifier of all defilements.
One cultivates that which cuts the bonds of the fetters;
beyond that, one finds no greater delight.
When the drum-like cloud thunders in the sky,
The torrents of rain fall everywhere along the path of the birds;
yet the bhikkhu, as if gone into a mountain cave,
meditates and finds no greater delight than that.
When he sits upon the banks of rivers filled with blossoms,
adorned with variegated garlands of woven cloth,
the noble-minded one meditates like a lotus.
Then one finds no greater delight than this:
when at midnight in the secluded forest,
while the rain is falling, the tusked beasts are roaring.
The bhikkhu meditates as if gone to a mountain cave;
from that, he finds no greater delight than this:
when he has restrained his own discursive thoughts.
Dwelling in a mountain cave within the forest,
free from fear and with all doubts dispelled, he meditates;
therefore, he finds no greater delight than that.
When one is happy, having destroyed all suffering and grief,
doorless, free from craving, and without taints;
when all cankers have been exhausted, one meditates.
“Beyond that, one finds no greater delight.
… Thus spoke the Elder Bhūta.
The Ninth Chapter is concluded.
In this regard, the summary verse is: Bhūta, Tathaddasa, Thera,
and one with the rhinoceros horn.
In the section on the ninefold [recitation],
these verses also consist of nine.
